difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: direct recall of what three standard methods are (dimensionality reduction, generative and discriminative models) with no computation, under a minute for a prepared student.
stem:
Match the items in **Column 1** with the items in **Column 2** in the following table:

| Column 1 | Column 2 |
| --- | --- |
| (p) Principal Component Analysis | (i) Discriminative Model |
| (q) Naïve Bayes Classification | (ii) Dimensionality Reduction |
| (r) Logistic Regression | (iii) Generative Model |

solution.quick: PCA projects data onto a few directions of maximum variance, so it is **dimensionality reduction** (ii). Naïve Bayes models $P(y)$ and $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$, the way the data are generated, and classifies with Bayes' rule, so it is **generative** (iii). Logistic regression models $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly, so it is **discriminative** (i). The matching (p)–(ii), (q)–(iii), (r)–(i) is **(C)**.

steps.title: Principal Component Analysis → Dimensionality Reduction
steps.body:
PCA is an unsupervised method. It computes the eigenvectors of the data covariance matrix and keeps the top $k$ directions (principal components), those with the largest variance. Each $d$-dimensional point is replaced by its $k$ coordinates along these directions, with $k < d$. PCA uses no class labels and does not predict $y$, so it is not a classifier at all. It matches **(ii) Dimensionality Reduction**.

Since the matching is one-to-one, (ii) can only go with PCA anyway: neither Naïve Bayes nor logistic regression reduces dimensionality.

steps.title: Recall generative vs discriminative
steps.body:
A probabilistic classifier needs $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$, and there are two ways to get it.

- **Generative model:** learn the joint distribution through $P(y)$ and $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$, i.e. how an example $\mathbf{x}$ is *generated* from each class, and then obtain the posterior with Bayes' rule (below).
- **Discriminative model:** learn $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$, or the decision boundary itself, directly, without modelling how $\mathbf{x}$ is distributed.

The Bayes' rule step used by a generative classifier is

$$
P(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)\,P(y)}{\sum_{y'} P(\mathbf{x} \mid y')\,P(y')} .
$$

steps.title: Naïve Bayes → Generative Model
steps.body:
Naïve Bayes estimates the class prior $P(y)$ and class-conditional distributions under the assumption that the features are conditionally independent given the class:

$$
P(\mathbf{x} \mid y) = \prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid y) .
$$

It then predicts $\hat{y} = \arg\max_y P(y)\prod_{j} P(x_j \mid y)$. Because it models $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$ and $P(y)$, and could even sample new feature vectors for a given class, it is a **(iii) Generative Model**.

steps.title: Logistic Regression → Discriminative Model
steps.body:
Logistic regression models the posterior directly:

$$
P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b)}} .
$$

Its parameters are fitted by maximising the conditional likelihood $\prod_i P(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i)$. Nothing about the distribution of $\mathbf{x}$ is modelled, so it is a **(i) Discriminative Model**.

steps.title: Assemble the matching
steps.body: (p) PCA – (ii), (q) Naïve Bayes – (iii), (r) Logistic Regression – (i). This is option **(C)**.

solution.teaching:
**Three different jobs in machine learning.** Column 1 lists three standard methods, and Column 2 describes what *kind* of method each is.

**Dimensionality reduction** reduces the number of features while keeping as much useful structure as possible. PCA does this by finding orthogonal directions of maximum variance, the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $\Sigma = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top$ with the largest eigenvalues, and projecting the data onto the top few. It is unsupervised: labels play no role.

**Generative vs discriminative classifiers.** Both aim to predict a label $y$ from features $\mathbf{x}$, but they model different things.

- A *generative* classifier builds a story of how the data arise: first a class $y$ is drawn with probability $P(y)$, then features are drawn from $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$. To classify, it inverts this story with Bayes' rule. Naïve Bayes is the textbook example; its "naïve" assumption, $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y) = \prod_j P(x_j \mid y)$, keeps the number of parameters small. Gaussian discriminant analysis (LDA/QDA) is another generative example.
- A *discriminative* classifier skips the story and models only what is needed for prediction: $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$ or the boundary between the classes. Logistic regression, $P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b)$, is the standard example; SVMs and most neural-network classifiers are also discriminative.

Naïve Bayes and logistic regression are the classic generative–discriminative pair: with binary features, or Gaussian features whose variances do not depend on the class, the Naïve Bayes posterior has the same sigmoid-of-linear form as logistic regression, but the parameters are obtained differently. Naïve Bayes fits $P(y)$ and $P(x_j \mid y)$ from counts or means, while logistic regression fits $\mathbf{w}$ directly by maximising $\prod_i P(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i)$.

**Back to the question:** PCA → dimensionality reduction, Naïve Bayes → generative, logistic regression → discriminative, which is option (C).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: (q) − (i) calls Naïve Bayes discriminative, but it models $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)P(y)$ and is generative. (r) − (ii) calls logistic regression dimensionality reduction, but it is a classifier that keeps all features. (p) − (iii) is also wrong, since PCA's role here is dimensionality reduction.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: (p) − (ii) is right, but the other two are swapped: Naïve Bayes is generative, not discriminative, and logistic regression is discriminative, not generative.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: PCA → Dimensionality Reduction, Naïve Bayes → Generative Model (it models $P(y)$ and $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$), and Logistic Regression → Discriminative Model (it models $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly). All three pairs are correct.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: (q) − (ii) calls Naïve Bayes a dimensionality-reduction method, which it is not: it is a classifier that uses every feature. (p) − (iii) is also wrong, since PCA is the only listed item that does dimensionality reduction. Only (r) − (i) is right.

solution.shortcut: Only PCA can be "Dimensionality Reduction", so (p) − (ii) leaves options (B) and (C). Naïve Bayes is the textbook generative classifier, so (q) − (iii) gives **(C)**.
solution.commonTrap: Deciding by the output instead of by what is modelled. Both Naïve Bayes and logistic regression output class probabilities $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$, so some students call both discriminative, or call logistic regression generative because it is "probabilistic". The test is whether the method models the distribution of the features, $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$: Naïve Bayes does (generative), logistic regression does not (discriminative).

PCA projects the data onto the top principal directions and is the only listed dimensionality-reduction method, so (p) − (ii). Naïve Bayes models P(y) and P(x | y) = ∏ P(x_j | y) and classifies with Bayes' rule, so it is generative: (q) − (iii). Logistic regression models P(y | x) = σ(wᵀx + b) directly, so it is discriminative: (r) − (i). This is option C. The question is purely conceptual, so no code check applies.
